title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
formal: For every fixed integer \(n\ge3\), is there a deterministic linearizable wait-free implementation of an unbounded FIFO queue for \(n\) asynchronous processes using only atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set objects?
definitions: Processes have distinct identifiers, arbitrary private memory and no timing information. The shared primitives are atomic registers supporting Read and Write of finite values, and test-and-set bits initially zero: TAS returns the old bit and sets it to one. An unbounded supply of fresh primitives is permitted; stronger atomic operations are not. Each process can repeatedly invoke either Enqueue(v), for any finite binary string \(v\), or Dequeue(). Sequential queue semantics append at the tail, remove and return the oldest item at the head, and return a distinguished empty marker immediately when empty. Linearizability requires each concurrent history to admit a sequential ordering of completed operations and a subset of pending operations that obeys these semantics and respects real-time precedence of nonoverlapping operations. Wait-freedom requires every operation of a process that continues taking steps to complete after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of delays or crashes of others. There is no restriction to designated enqueuers or dequeuers and no bound on the number of operations. Algorithms may depend on \(n\); they receive no random coins.
why: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.

context_blocks.text: Stacks belong to Common2, but this does not give a queue implementation. Restricted one- or two-enqueuer/dequeuer queues leave the unrestricted many-process interface unresolved.
The source explicitly identifies the open question with an n-process linearizable wait-free queue built from test-and-set and registers. Lock-free system-wide progress is a weaker guarantee.

sentences: Several processes concurrently insert and remove items from a FIFO queue.
Every continuing process must complete its own operation despite arbitrary delays of others.
Only read/write registers and test-and-set primitives are available.
Known restricted queue implementations do not cover the full interface.
The question separates the synchronization power of a queue from that of weaker shared objects.
